name: Glenohumeral Instability

tests.patientPosition: Supine (more secure) or sitting; arm abducted to 90 degrees, elbow bent to 90 degrees
tests.therapistPosition: Beside the shoulder; one hand supports the elbow, the other the wrist
procedure: Slowly rotate the arm outward (external rotation), stopping at the first sign of apprehension or at end range

tests.name: Relocation (Jobe) test
tests.purpose: Check whether a posterior force on the humeral head reduces apprehension
tests.patientPosition: Supine, same arm position as E1
procedure: At the point where apprehension occurs, apply a gentle posteriorly directed force to the front of the humeral head, then see if the patient can rotate further with less apprehension

blocks.text: The shoulder is the most mobile joint in the body. A shallow socket (glenoid) holds a large ball (humeral head), so stability depends on the labrum, ligaments, capsule and the rotator cuff and scapular muscles. **Glenohumeral instability** means the joint cannot keep the ball centred during activity. It ranges from **subluxation** (partial slip) to **dislocation** (complete loss of contact).

rows: A fall or collision with the arm out to the side and rotated outward; often a young, active person; may involve labral tear or bone injury
Loose joint in several directions, often in people with generalised joint hypermobility; symptoms with everyday or sports use; no major injury
Less common; may follow seizure, electric shock, or repeated pushing or loading with the arm forward

blocks.text: After a first traumatic anterior dislocation in young active people, the chance of another dislocation is high [Ref - to verify]. Older patients are less likely to redislocate but more likely to have a rotator cuff tear or fracture [Ref - to verify].

sections.title: H. Working diagnosis and decision pathway

items: Acute deformity or neurovascular signs? **Yes:** emergency pathway.
History of dislocation or slipping plus apprehension and relocation signs? **Yes:** working diagnosis is anterior glenohumeral instability.
Generalised laxity, no major injury, symptoms in several directions? **Yes:** working diagnosis is multidirectional or atraumatic instability; first line is rehabilitation.

Young, active, first-time traumatic dislocation, or recurrent dislocations, or high-demand contact sport? **Yes:** discuss an orthopaedic opinion early, because surgery may be considered [Ref - to verify].
Otherwise: begin rehabilitation and monitor.

blocks.text: **Preferred starting choice:** rehabilitation, not manual therapy. Do not stretch or mobilise the capsule of an unstable shoulder. Avoid forcing end-range external rotation. Manual therapy has a small supporting role only (comfort, thoracic mobility).

sections.title: J. Exercise prescription (example starting plan, not universal)

blocks.text: **Principle:** build the dynamic stability of the cuff and scapular muscles in positions the patient can control, then progress toward the position of instability and sport demands. Programs for atraumatic instability usually follow a long, structured plan [Ref - to verify].

rows: Elbow at side, push into a wall or hand
Banded external and internal rotation at the side; rows; serratus punches
Elbow at the side, light band
Scaption, quadruped weight shift, closed-chain loading
Plyometric catches, overhead loading, contact preparation

blocks.text: **Avoid early:** end-range external rotation with abduction (the position of instability), forceful stretches, and unsupervised heavy contact sport.

**Return to sport criteria (example):** no apprehension, strength and endurance close to the other side, confident sport-specific movements, and agreement with the medical team. Use objective measures where available; no fixed time is stated [Ref - to verify].

rows: Proprioceptive cue or temporary protection in sport; limited evidence [Ref - to verify]

blocks.text: A sling after a first dislocation is typically short-term; the best position and duration are debated [Ref - to verify]. Follow the treating doctor's instruction.

items: **Acute:** refer for reduction and imaging. Protect the shoulder, manage pain, check nerves and vessels.
**Early rehabilitation:** restore pain-free movement within safe limits, begin isometrics and scapular work.
**Strengthening:** progress rotator cuff, scapular and trunk strengthening.
**Control and sport-specific work:** train control in positions of risk gradually.

**Decision point:** for recurrent instability, a young active patient or a bone defect, discuss surgery (for example labral repair) with an orthopaedic surgeon. Rehabilitation continues before and after surgery.

blocks.text: **Case:** A 20-year-old rugby player dislocated his right shoulder 3 weeks ago and it was reduced in hospital. He now has apprehension when the arm is abducted and rotated outward, and the relocation test reduces it. Sensation over the lateral upper arm is normal and the deltoid contracts well. He wants to return to rugby in 6 weeks.

**Working diagnosis:** anterior glenohumeral instability after traumatic dislocation. **Plan:** rehabilitation with progressive strengthening and control, avoid forced external rotation positions, and an early orthopaedic discussion about the risk of recurrence in a young contact athlete. Set return criteria rather than a fixed date.

items: Why is pain alone not a positive apprehension test? The test is meant to reproduce the feeling of impending slipping. Pain can come from many structures and does not identify instability.
Why do we check the deltoid and lateral arm sensation after a dislocation? The axillary nerve can be injured, and the finding changes referral urgency and rehabilitation.
Why not stretch the capsule in MDI? The problem is too much looseness, so stretching is more likely to worsen it. Strength and control are the target.
A 55-year-old cannot lift the arm after dislocation. What is suspected? A rotator cuff tear, so refer for early imaging.
Why discuss surgery early in this player? Young contact athletes have a high redislocation risk, so the surgeon and patient should discuss the options early [Ref - to verify].
**Initial approach:** safe medical care for acute injury, then rehabilitation.
**Justifying findings:** apprehension, relocation, history, nerve status.
**Priority:** dynamic stability and confidence.
**Manual therapy:** minor role; avoid capsular stretching.
**Exercise:** isometrics, cuff and scapular strengthening, control drills, sport-specific work.
**Modalities:** limited role.
**Tell the patient:** many shoulders stabilise with training, some need surgery; report new numbness or repeated dislocation.
**Avoid:** forced external rotation, premature return to contact sport.
**Measure:** apprehension, strength, function, WOSI.
**If no improvement:** orthopaedic opinion.
**Referral triggers:** Section G.
**Discharge:** return criteria met and maintenance program in place.

blocks.text: **Assumptions:** no fracture or nerve injury, acute care complete.

items: **Can be tested:** whether early surgery or rehabilitation gives fewer recurrences in young athletes; accuracy of apprehension and relocation tests.
**Hypotheses:** that rehabilitation improves dynamic stability by better neuromuscular control.
**Future questions:** the best rehabilitation program for multidirectional instability, and optimal sling position.
